title: Canadian power, water and fibre screening candidates
methodology: Hydroelectric and nuclear generation context is paired with city-level municipal water metrics and any sourced fibre evidence. These comparisons do not prove that a local substation, transmission corridor, carrier route, water source, or permit can support a new load. The locations are candidates for utility-led feasibility studies, not approved sites.

rows.powerFact: Hydro-Québec reports 152.672 TWh of hydropower generation in 2025 and 37.371 GW of total installed generating-station capacity (all source types).
rows.powerScaleComparison: A 100 MW continuous load is 876 GWh/year, about 0.57% of Hydro-Québec’s 2025 hydropower generation; this is a provincial scale comparison.
rows.gridAndPolicyFact: Hydro-Québec says data centres currently use about 200 MW and could exceed 1,000 MW by 2035; projects over 5 MW are selected, and a proposed C$0.13/kWh rate is subject to regulatory approval.
rows.municipalWaterFact: Montréal reports 1.6 billion litres/day produced from the St. Lawrence, Lac Saint-Louis and Rivière des Prairies; this is city-wide production, not unallocated industrial capacity.
rows.assessment: Strong provincial hydro and urban water context; a 100 MW connection would still require utility selection and a site-specific grid study.
rows.openQuestion: Quebec City and Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean are alternate corridors to screen; municipal water capacity and firm transmission for a specific campus are not established here.

rows.powerFact: Manitoba Hydro reports 6.074 GW net generating capability across its system, with nearly all annual electricity generation from 16 hydro stations; most hydroelectric output comes from northern stations.
rows.powerScaleComparison: 100 MW is about 1.65% of Manitoba Hydro’s 6.074 GW net generating capability; this compares nameplate capacity, not uncommitted supply.
rows.gridAndPolicyFact: The 2025–26 annual report says drought reduced hydro generation and required larger power imports; that is a reminder that hydro output and exportable surplus vary with water conditions.
rows.municipalWaterFact: Winnipeg's water-treatment plant is designed for 400 million litres/day; this is plant design capacity, not free cooling-water allocation.
rows.assessment: Strong hydro/water resource screen and a major urban service base; regional transmission and drought-adjusted firm supply need confirmation.
rows.openQuestion: A 100 MW campus is about 1.6% of Manitoba Hydro's reported generating capability; this comparison does not imply 100 MW is uncommitted or deliverable in Winnipeg.

rows.powerFact: BC Hydro generated 40.860 TWh from hydro in fiscal 2025; hydroelectric installations account for over 80% of BC Hydro's installed generating capacity.
rows.powerScaleComparison: A 100 MW continuous load is 876 GWh/year, about 2.14% of BC Hydro’s FY2025 hydropower generation; it would also equal one quarter of the 400 MW maximum allocation in the 2026 call.
rows.gridAndPolicyFact: BC Hydro's 2026 emerging-industries call allocates up to 400 MW province-wide to storage and AI data centres, showing that hydro-richness does not mean spare local capacity is available to any one project.
rows.gridAndPolicySource: BC Hydro 2026 Call for Demand Q&A
rows.municipalWaterFact: Prince George reported 11.333 million m³ of water supplied in 2023 (about 31.1 million litres/day on average), drawn from municipal groundwater wells; this is an annual average, not a guaranteed new industrial allocation.
rows.waterSource: City of Prince George 2023 water-system report
rows.assessment: Hydro-rich provincial system and a city water network make this a candidate for screening, but BC Hydro's allocation process and regional transmission are material constraints.
rows.openQuestion: A 100 MW campus would consume about 2.3% of Prince George's 2023 average municipal water production at the 0.3 L/kWh planning WUE; confirm seasonal source yield and permits.

rows.powerFact: Bruce Power's existing eight-unit site near Tiverton produces about 6,550 MW of peak output. Ontario has supported pre-development work for Bruce C, a proposed expansion of up to 4,800 MW; the project remains in federal impact assessment and there is no decision to build a new station.
rows.powerScaleComparison: A 100 MW continuous campus equals about 1.5% of Bruce Power's current 6,550 MW peak output. This is a scale comparison only; current plant output does not establish a power contract, spare supply, or deliverable capacity for a separate campus.
rows.gridAndPolicyFact: The IESO's August 2026 bulk plan models about 12 GW of generation under the Bruce C scenario and finds that existing transmission cannot fully deliver that output under the study conditions. New 500 kV lines to Longwood and Essa are future-consideration projects triggered by Bruce C in the 2040s. The IESO also notes that new customer loads near generation can reduce transfers across an interface, while loads sited at or near an interface can worsen constraints. Co-location is therefore a grid hypothesis to study, not proof of a power connection. This expansion export constraint does not determine whether a new local data-centre load can connect today.
rows.gridAndPolicySource: IESO South and Central Bulk Plan (August 2026)
rows.municipalWaterFact: The Bruce Power site is beside Lake Huron, but this screen does not establish a data centre's permitted water supply, withdrawal, or discharge capacity. Existing nuclear plant water systems are not assumed to be available to another operator.
rows.waterSource: Bruce C impact assessment and cooling-water planning
rows.communicationsFact: Bruce Telecom reported all Tiverton homes fibre-ready in 2024 and advertises address-dependent business service up to 1 Gbps symmetrical. Execulink advertises fibre up to 3 Gbps in Owen Sound, subject to address availability. These retail services show fibre access in the region but do not establish campus-scale backhaul, dark fibre, route diversity, or carrier redundancy. Owen Sound is about 68 km by road from Tiverton, so it is a separate power-connection location rather than a co-located load.
rows.assessment: Tiverton merits an energy-adjacent regional-compute pre-feasibility study. Owen Sound may be a regional alternative with its own fibre and utility connection, but should be assessed as a separate load node. Neither location is currently verified for a frontier-scale campus.
rows.openQuestion: Confirm a parcel-level high-voltage connection, firm supply and commercial structure, local distribution capacity, carrier-grade fibre capacity and physically diverse routes, cooling-water source and permits, land and municipal readiness. Bruce C is within Saugeen Ojibway Nation territory; Indigenous rights-holder engagement is central to any project.
